prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "APPLIED MATERIALS INC /DE" (ticker AMAT), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "AMAT", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Applied Materials, Inc.
result.industry: Semiconductor manufacturing equipment (wafer fab equipment and services)
markets: Deposition equipment (CVD, PVD, ALD, epitaxy, electroplating)
Process control: e-beam inspection and metrology
Applied Global Services: spares, upgrades, service subscriptions

mission.statement: We deliver material innovation that changes the world.
mission.source: Applied Materials company website, About page (headline statement; the company also uses the tagline “Make Possible a Better Future”)
mission.plain: Applied Materials invents new ways to build and shape materials so chips and screens keep getting better.

about.plain: Applied Materials builds the giant machines that chip factories use to make computer chips. Its machines lay down super-thin layers of material, carve them away, and check the results, all at the scale of atoms. Almost every new chip in the world has passed through its machines. It also earns money fixing, upgrading and supplying parts for the thousands of machines already in factories.
about.customers: Chipmakers such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK hynix and Micron, plus Chinese chipmakers and display makers.
about.everyday: The chips in your phone, laptop and the AI servers behind ChatGPT were almost certainly made using Applied Materials machines.

money.plain: deposition, etch, implant, CMP and inspection tools
spare parts, upgrades, service contracts and AIx software
machines for making TV and phone screens
hybrid bonding and HBM stacking machines for AI chips
a large new Silicon Valley R&D hub where chipmakers develop new technology with Applied

result.summary: Applied Materials has a wide moat built on the broadest product portfolio in chip equipment, deep materials-engineering know-how (over 23,500 patents and about $3.6B of yearly R&D) and high switching costs once its tools are qualified into a chipmaker's process. Its installed base feeds a growing, high-margin service business (Applied Global Services, $6.4B in FY2025). The advantage is real but shared with a small oligopoly (Lam, Tokyo Electron, KLA, ASML), and the business stays cyclical and exposed to China.

pricingPower.evidence: Gross margin rose from 44.7% in FY2020 to 48.7% in FY2025 and 50.3% in Q3 FY2026 (13th straight quarter of year-over-year gross margin expansion), but revenue still swings with chipmakers' capital spending and it shares most markets with Lam and Tokyo Electron.

moats.evidence: Over 23,500 patents and a reputation as the leader in materials engineering; its brand matters to chipmakers' engineers, not consumers.

Once a tool is qualified into a chipmaker's process recipe, replacing it risks yield loss and months of requalification; over 37,000 installed chambers are connected to its AIx software and feed recurring AGS revenue.
Data from its large installed base and EPIC co-development partners improves its tools, but there is no true user network effect.
As the largest broad-line equipment maker by revenue ($28.4B in FY2025) it spreads about $3.6B of R&D and a global service force over more product lines than any rival.
Each equipment niche supports only two or three qualified suppliers, so new entrants struggle to win enough volume, except Chinese firms backed by the state.
Its integrated co-optimized solutions (combining several process steps) are hard for single-product rivals to match, but incumbents can respond.
Decades of atomic-scale materials know-how across deposition, etch, implant and inspection let it ship enabling tools for gate-all-around transistors, backside power and HBM packaging.
It has no exclusive asset like ASML's EUV, though its EPIC Center and engineering workforce of about 36,500 employees are valuable.

customers.evidence: Long relationships with every major chipmaker (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK hynix, Micron); AGS service revenue grew 22% year over year to a record $1.78B in Q3 FY2026, showing customers keep buying upgrades and subscriptions on its installed base.

talent.evidence: About 36,500 employees; named a LinkedIn Top Company (San Francisco, 2026) but ranked only #601 in Forbes World's Best Employers 2026 (#377 in 2025).

product.evidence: Market leader in deposition (CVD, PVD, epitaxy), CMP and ion implant, with recent launches such as the Centura Prime Epi for DRAM and Producer Avila for HBM; Lam leads in etch and ASML in lithography.

competitors.name: Lam Research Corporation
competitors.note: Etch and deposition (CVD, ALD, electroplating), especially in memory.

competitors.name: Tokyo Electron Limited
competitors.note: Deposition, etch, thermal processing, cleaning and coater/developers.

competitors.name: KLA Corporation
competitors.note: Process control: inspection and metrology versus Applied's e-beam tools.

competitors.name: ASM International N.V.
competitors.note: ALD and epitaxy deposition for leading-edge logic.

competitors.name: Kokusai Electric Corporation
competitors.note: Batch deposition and thermal processing, especially for memory.

competitors.name: NAURA Technology Group
competitors.note: Chinese maker of deposition, etch and thermal tools, gaining share in China.

competitors.name: Axcelis Technologies, Inc.
competitors.note: Ion implantation, especially for power and mature nodes.

competitors.name: ASML Holding N.V.
competitors.note: Lithography; competes for chipmakers' equipment budgets and in e-beam metrology.

competitors.name: SCREEN Holdings Co., Ltd.
competitors.note: Wafer cleaning and some thermal processing.

competitors.name: Hitachi High-Tech Corporation
competitors.note: Etch and CD-SEM metrology; owned by Hitachi.

competitors.name: Piotech Inc.
competitors.note: Chinese CVD and ALD deposition supplier.

competitors.name: BE Semiconductor Industries (Besi)
competitors.note: Hybrid bonding for advanced packaging (Applied is also a partner and shareholder).

threats: China was 30% of FY2025 revenue ($8,529M) and 26% in Q3 FY2026; tighter US export controls can cut sales, as the 2025 rule change and the $252.5M BIS settlement (February 2026) showed
State-backed Chinese rivals (NAURA, AMEC, Piotech) are replacing foreign tools in China
Lam Research and Tokyo Electron gained share in etch and deposition in 2025 according to The Information Network
Cyclical chipmaker capital spending; a pause in AI data-center or memory investment would hit orders
Heavy customer concentration in TSMC, Samsung, Intel and a few memory makers
Shifts in chip architecture (e.g. more etch-heavy 3D NAND or lithography-led scaling) could move spending toward rivals

ceo.name: Gary E. Dickerson
ceo.background: BS in engineering management (University of Missouri-Rolla), MBA (University of Missouri-Kansas City); 18 years at KLA-Tencor (rising to president and COO), then CEO of Varian Semiconductor until Applied bought it in 2011

c1.evidence: Applied is the largest broad-line chip-equipment maker ($28.4B FY2025 revenue), but chipmaking equipment is a mature, cyclical industry rather than an emerging one, even though AI is now driving fast growth (Q3 FY2026 revenue +25%).

c2.evidence: Chipmakers choose it for the broadest materials-engineering portfolio and co-optimized process steps (e.g. gate-all-around, HBM packaging), backed by decades of know-how and qualified recipes that are hard to copy.

c3.evidence: It is the default name in deposition and materials engineering inside the chip industry, but ordinary consumers rarely know Applied Materials.

c4.evidence: It repeats “Make Possible a Better Future” and “material innovation that changes the world” and enabling AI chips matters, but its messaging is mostly about technology leadership and financial targets.

c6.evidence: “chip equipment, cyclical, AI supplier”; among investors and engineers the impression is mostly positive, though recent news has also focused on China export-control problems.

c7.evidence: Wafer fab equipment is a market of over $100B (TechInsights put total IC manufacturing equipment at $136.2B in 2025, +13%) riding the AI build-out, and Applied guides record Q4 FY2026 revenue of $10.25B (+51%).

c8.evidence: It is expanding into advanced packaging (revenue expected up more than 70% in calendar 2026), process control (expected up more than 50%) and AIx software-based services.

m1.evidence: Dickerson has long articulated an ‘AI era’ driven by materials innovation and built the EPIC co-development center around it, but he is a strategist-operator rather than a famous visionary.

m2.evidence: Not a founder, but in 13 years as CEO he has made long-term bets such as the EPIC Center and a high-velocity co-innovation model.

m4.evidence: He emphasises partnership with customers (one of Applied's four values) and co-development, with no notable evidence of servant-leadership style beyond that.

m5.evidence: He reorganised Applied around faster co-innovation with customers and records over 23,500 patents, but the culture is not widely seen as distinctive.

m6.evidence: An engineering-management graduate who spent 18 years in operations and product development at KLA-Tencor and ran Varian Semiconductor, he is deeply versed in the technology.

m7.evidence: No public evidence either way beyond a conventional executive record; Applied paid a $252.5M settlement in 2026 over 2020-2022 China shipments under his tenure.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Gary Dickerson giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Dickerson is a low-profile industry executive without a widely known public persona.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2013, revenue reached a record $28,368M in FY2025, its sixth consecutive year of growth, and gross margin rose to 50.3% in Q3 FY2026.

m10.evidence: No notable public reputation for frugality; the company is investing heavily, with capex rising to $2,260M in FY2025.

c10.evidence: Its machines help make almost every new chip, so phones, computers, cars and AI services used by billions of people depend on them.

p2.evidence: Depositing and shaping films a few atoms thick across billions of transistors is extremely hard, and it is essential to all modern electronics.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 44.7% (FY2020) to 48.7% (FY2025) and operating margin from 25.4% to 29.2%, though operating margin dipped from 30.2% in FY2022.

f3.evidence: At July 26, 2026 debt was $6,544M against $9,233M of cash and short-term investments (plus $5,268M long-term investments) and TTM operating cash flow of about $8.4B, with equity of $25,626M.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $4,365M (FY2020) to $8,289M (FY2025) and operating cash flow from $3,804M to $7,958M, although cash flow peaked at $8,700M in FY2023.

v1.evidence: Applied leads in deposition, CMP and implant, but rivals lead elsewhere (Lam in etch, KLA in inspection, ASML in lithography), so it is not clearly best in every field.

v2.evidence: It was named a LinkedIn Top Company (San Francisco, 2026) but ranked #601 in Forbes World's Best Employers 2026 and #370 in TIME World's Best Companies 2025.

c5.evidence: If Applied vanished, chipmakers like TSMC, Samsung and Intel could not build or maintain many fabs, delaying phones, PCs, cars and AI data centers worldwide.
